title: The Michael Jackson Biopic Just Crossed $700 Million — and India Is a Bigger Reason Than You Think
excerpt: Jaafar Jackson's 'Michael' has earned ₹67 crore in India alone, making it the second-highest-grossing Hollywood film of 2026 in the country — and it's not done yet
body:
There's a moment in Antoine Fuqua's *Michael* — the one where Jaafar Jackson, playing his uncle, first moonwalks across a stage lit like a cathedral — that has been making entire Indian theatre audiences erupt. Not polite clapping. Full-throated, whistling, "interval-level" eruptions. Four weeks into its run, the Michael Jackson biopic has crossed $700 million at the global box office, and India's contribution to that number tells a story all its own.

## The Numbers Don't Lie

*Michael* earned $703 million worldwide by the end of its fourth weekend — $282 million domestic, $421 million overseas. It reclaimed the #1 spot at the US box office with $26.1 million, pushing past *The Devil Wears Prada 2*. Japan hasn't even opened yet. The film is now gunning for *Bohemian Rhapsody*'s $911 million record as the highest-grossing music biopic of all time.

But the Indian numbers are what deserve attention. The biopic has grossed ₹67.55 crore ($8 million) in India through 25 days — making it the **second-highest-grossing Hollywood film of 2026** in the country, behind only *Project Hail Mary*. It's projected to close between ₹75–80 crore, a number that puts it in genuinely rare company for a non-superhero, non-franchise Hollywood film in India.

## Why India Can't Get Enough of MJ

Michael Jackson's hold on India was never about one hit. It was generational infrastructure. Every school dance competition from Trivandrum to Chandigarh in the 1990s had a kid attempting the moonwalk. "Thriller" played at Diwali parties. "Billie Jean" was the unofficial soundtrack of every New Year's Eve countdown on Doordarshan. When Jackson died in 2009, Indian television networks ran wall-to-wall coverage that rivalled their own national events.

So when Fuqua's biopic landed in Indian multiplexes on April 24, it wasn't selling nostalgia to a niche audience. It was tapping into something embedded in the country's pop-culture DNA. Morning shows in Mumbai sold out. Weekend occupancy in Bengaluru and Chennai consistently hit 75-84%. Tier-2 cities like Jaipur and Lucknow showed stronger-than-usual holdover, unusual for a Hollywood release beyond its opening week.

## Jaafar Jackson's Uncanny Turn

The film's secret weapon is casting. Jaafar Jackson — Michael's nephew, son of Jermaine — doesn't just play the role. He physically *becomes* the King of Pop, performing every dance sequence without a body double and singing several tracks himself. Critics who walked in sceptical about the estate-approved biopic walked out conceding that the performance transcends the project's more sanitised storytelling choices. The 95-97% audience score on review aggregators tells the story: whatever you think of the film's narrative choices, the spectacle delivers.

Nia Long as Katherine Jackson and Colman Domingo as Joe Jackson ground the family drama, while the concert recreations — particularly the Motown 25 performance and the *Bad* world tour sequences — are staged with the kind of scale that demands a theatre screen.

## The NRI Angle: Streaming Waits, Theatre Wins

Here's the irony for diaspora audiences: while *Michael* is dominating Indian multiplexes, NRIs in the US, UK, and Canada have had to compete with Hollywood's own crowded release calendar for screens. The film opened to $97.2 million domestically — a record for a music biopic — but IMAX and premium screens were in high demand.

For Indian-Americans and British Indians who grew up in households where MJ was the one Western artist their parents also loved, *Michael* is landing as a shared cultural event. Group bookings at AMC and Cineworld locations in Edison, Hounslow, and Brampton have reportedly spiked, with community WhatsApp groups coordinating weekend outings — the kind of collective experience usually reserved for a Rajinikanth release or a cricket World Cup screening.

## Can It Beat Bohemian Rhapsody?

At $703 million and climbing, *Michael* needs another $208 million to dethrone *Bohemian Rhapsody* ($911 million). With Japan's release still ahead and strong holds across Asia and Latin America, box office analysts give it a realistic shot — though it'll need to sustain momentum through June. India alone could add another ₹10-15 crore to the tally if word-of-mouth holds.

What's already clear: Hollywood just proved, again, that India doesn't need superheroes to show up in numbers. Give them a legend, a performance worth the ticket price, and a story their parents will understand — and they'll fill the seats.
